title: Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects within Reusable Logic with Composables. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Extracting a composable helps multiple components share behavior without coupling their visual markup.

content_blocks.title: Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects: Server rendering and hydration
content_blocks.alt_text: Server rendering and hydration diagram for lesson 69: Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects. Render deterministic HTML for this request → Send markup without shared mutable user state → Attach events to matching initial output
content_blocks.caption: Rendering flow: server output and client hydration must agree, and per-request state must remain isolated.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Composables are reusable functions that package stateful Composition API logic such as data fetching, form rules, and browser subscriptions. This lesson focuses on Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Lifecycle hooks inside composables
items.text: For Lifecycle hooks inside composables, place DOM or external-system work in the lifecycle phase where the needed element exists, then clean up timers, listeners, observers, or subscriptions when the component no longer needs them. Use nextTick() when code must wait for Vue's queued DOM update.

items.title: Cleaning up event listeners
items.text: For Cleaning up event listeners, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Watcher cleanup
items.text: For Watcher cleanup, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Preventing stale asynchronous results
items.text: For Preventing stale asynchronous results, model pending, success, empty, and failure states. Check HTTP status before treating a response as success, cancel stale work where appropriate, and do not let a late response overwrite newer user intent.

items.title: SSR-compatible composables
items.text: For SSR-compatible composables, decide which code runs during build, on the server, and in the browser. Keep output deterministic during hydration, isolate state per server request, keep secrets server-only, and test the actual production build rather than relying only on the dev server.

content_blocks.expected_output: Each caller gets a counter initialized from its argument and a doubled computed value; increment changes both display values reactively.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Create the composable in a JavaScript file and import it in <script setup>. Call composables synchronously inside setup context.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Cleaning up event listeners”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Composables are reusable functions that package stateful Composition API logic such as data fetching, form rules, and browser subscriptions. For Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects” that applies “Lifecycle hooks inside composables”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Lifecycle hooks inside composables”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Composable Lifecycle and Side Effects belongs to the broader area Reusable Logic with Composables.
The main concept to practice is Lifecycle hooks inside composables.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
